newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfricans rescue dying animals from shipment.
newsitem.headline: SAfricans rescue dying animals from shipment.

text.p: South African zoo officials on Wednesday nursed survivors among 2,500 exotic creatures found suffocating in a shipment destined for the U.S. pet market.
Hundreds of chameleons, snakes, lizards, geckos, tortoises, spiders and scorpions in the shipment from Mozambique had died before they were discovered at Johannesburg's international airport.

Rick Allan, a senior inspector with the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SPCA), said the shipment had the required certificates of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES).

"This shipment is perfectly legal according to the nature conservation requirements for each country and for the CITES permits...But the one thing the people have neglected is the actual welfare of the animals," he told Reuters at Pretoria zoo.

Fighting off a cloud of flies amid the stench, Allan showed how four adult chameleons had been sardined into a container half the size of a shoe box. The hollow eye sockets of two dead chameleons squashed on top of each other stared out.
"There weren't enough airholes, so the one bit its way through the partition, suffocated the other chameleon and then also died because it still couldn't get enough air."
Smaller boxes were stacked on top of each other in about 30 large containers, also lacking adequate ventilation.

Helpless animals -- including a scorpion with her young clamouring on her back -- clawed for air in tiny boxes Allan hauled from the larger containers. Chameleons, dehydrated almost to skin and bone, lapped up a fine mist sprayed over plants where they were recovering.
Allan said he was tipped off about the animals while he was confiscating 30 parrots, also from Mozambique, packed into a bird cage.
Another 2,000 animals had already been flown to the United States, destined for shops in Hollywood, Florida, according to the packaging label.
"This is only one of many sub-standard examples of animals arriving in transit at international airports," Allan said.

Those that survived may have to repeat the journey. A state quarantine officer allowed the zoo to care for the animals only until Friday -- when they must be returned to the owner in Mozambique who packaged them, and can reship them.
